Seminole. A Southeast nation formed in the eighteenth century from Creek and other Southeastern peoples in the Florida peninsula. They are known for their distinctive patchwork clothing, cypress-dome settlements, and fierce resistance during the Seminole Wars, successfully defying forced removal longer than most Eastern tribes before resettling in Oklahoma and Florida reservations.

The name Seminole derives from Spanish cimarrón, meaning "wild" or "runaway," referring to people who separated from the Creek Nation. They absorbed Creek, Yamassee, and escaped slaves fleeing oppression. The Seminole constructed unique dwellings called chickees—open-sided, thatched-roof structures adapted to Florida's swampy terrain and hot climate. They created distinctive clothing traditions, especially women's patchwork skirts and woven sashes, made with colorful traded textiles.

The Seminole resisted forced removal in the Seminole Wars from 1817 to 1858. Osceola led guerrilla resistance against Andrew Jackson and U.S. forces in the Second Seminole War from 1835 to 1842. A group of Seminoles, led by Billy Bowlegs, successfully evaded forced removal, and their descendants remain in the Florida Everglades as the Seminole Tribe of Florida.

Today two federally recognized Seminole nations exist: the Seminole Tribe of Florida and the Seminole Nation of Oklahoma, both maintaining strong tribal governments and cultural traditions. They remain connected to the memory of the Seminole Wars and to the legacy of removal-era resistance.
